findings.title: toASCII/toUnicode silently drop everything after a second '@'
findings.property: converting an address/domain must not lose characters: an ASCII-only input is returned unchanged
findings.property_test: toASCII/toUnicode preserve text outside the domain in emails with several @
findings.expected: 'a@b@c' (already ASCII, so unchanged; only the domain part is punycoded)
findings.actual: 'a@b' (the '@c' suffix is silently discarded; toUnicode has the same behaviour)
findings.evidence: Docs say 'Only the non-ASCII parts of the domain name will be converted, i.e. it doesn't matter if you call it with a domain that's already in ASCII', and mapDomain says 'Leave the local part (i.e. everything up to `@`) intact'. mapDomain uses domain.split('@') and only keeps parts[0] and parts[1], so parts[2..] are lost. Quoted local parts may legally contain '@' (RFC 5321), so this is data loss rather than a rejected input.

error.message:
Expected values to be strictly equal:

'a@b' !== 'a@b@c'

review.title: punycode.toASCII/toUnicode truncate input containing more than one '@'
review.reason: mapDomain does `domain.split('@')` and uses only parts[0] and parts[1], so any further segments are silently dropped. `toASCII('a@b@c')` returns `'a@b'`, losing characters from an already-ASCII input, which contradicts the docs saying already-ASCII input is fine. A valid RFC 5321 address with a quoted local part, such as `"a@b"@例え.jp`, is also mangled: the real domain is lost and never punycoded. Splitting on the last '@' (`lastIndexOf`) is a small, safe fix. The case is rare and the library is in maintenance mode, so a maintainer might treat it as low priority.
